a2bbe9fb682a.title: Adapting Guidelines for Country use
a2bbe9fb682a.content: . The following page provides a reference to resources that can guide countries in adapting the guidelines for country use. To implement WHO recommendations in country settings, governments must interpret and then adapt the content in line with local policies, procedures, and digital tools. This implementation guide provides the generic content required in digital systems, independently of a specific software application and with the intention that countries can adapt it to meet local needs. WHO guidelines articulate and endorse rigorously tested recommendations for health interventions to be adopted within country programs. When applied correctly and consistently, guideline recommendations save lives. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from digital health investments, the SMART Guidelines approach is intended to facilitate the accurate reflection of WHO’s clinical, public health and data use guidelines in the digital systems that countries are adopting. For more on layers of knowledge representation and how they are used in WHO’s SMART Guidelines approach, see WHO’s SMART Guidelines and this Lancet article. The standards-based technical artifacts in this implementation guide are at the third layer of knowledge representation (L3: Machine-readable recommendations). It provides code necessary for software developers to incorporate standardised logic from WHO guidelines into digital systems, testable for conformance to standards including fidelity to recommendations. A standards-based technical implementation guide builds on operational (L2) by mapping L2 content to value sets and Health Level Seven International Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards. Alongside data standards from L2, this allows for semantic and syntactic interoperability at scale. The logic derived from guidelines, which might include clinical decision support and calculations for performance indicators, which may be encoded into Clinical Quality Language (CQL). This ensures that key indicators can be consistently extracted to support patient care, as well as case surveillance and programme monitoring. The machine-readable representations in this implementation guide are intended for adaptation into countries’ digital health service delivery and reporting systems. Digital solutions comprising L3 machine-readable recommendations may then be testable for conformance to interoperability standards. The fourth layer (L4: Executable—reference applications and services) focuses on software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. It is intended to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions, operational, and functional requirements of the WHO recommendations; addresses user and health system needs; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in the L1–L3 layers. As a fully functional application, it is intended to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be localised to the specific operational context of the users, population, and health system within which it is deployed. Additional products at this layer include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability; reusable software libraries including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and function as a service to support updates to FHIR content and capabilities across subscribed digital systems. Edit this page on GitHub .

5273b21059d4.title: Business Processes
5273b21059d4.content: . This page describes the core business processes and workflows for the Personal Health Wallet (PHW) Implementation Guide, integrating IHE IT Infrastructure Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) v1.1.0 (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/1.1.0/) and IHE IT Infrastructure Verifiable Health Links (VHL) v1.0.0-comment (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/1.0.0-comment/). A business process is a set of related activities or tasks performed together by system actors and human personas to achieve a health information exchange objective. Each workflow below is authored in BPMN 2.0 (input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn) with full BPMN Diagram Interchange (bpmndi:BPMNDiagram) layout and drawn from it to SVG (input/images/PHW.A.svg and so on) by tools/render-bpmn/render_bpmn.ts; never edit a drawing, change the BPMN. The data sharing agreement processes D to H, below, take the same form. Architectural Principles . | Trust-Anchor Neutrality: Every process models PKI key publication ([ITI-YY1]) and trust list retrieval ([ITI-YY2]) against an abstract Trust Anchor actor (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ActorDefinition/TrustAnchor). The WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) is one possible Trust Anchor implementation among others (such as national health PKI roots, regional cross-border trust networks, or bilateral federation anchors). | Explicit IHE PCF and VHL Transaction Binding: Every cross-actor task names its normative IHE transaction ([ITI-108] Access Consent, [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID, [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID, [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL, [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL, [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest). | No IHE IUA Claim: Consent management and enforcement operate over IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent and VHL [ITI-YY1]–[ITI-YY5] without claiming conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA [ITI-71]). | | Three-Valued Consent Decision and PROV-O Provenance: During VHL redemption (Process C), patient privacy consent directives retrieved via [ITI-108] are translated to W3C ODRL 2.2 policies (consentToOdrl()) and evaluated via three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown), recording a W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . | . Overview of Key Business Processes . The following table summarizes the three BPMN 2.0 consent and Verifiable Health Link business processes defined in this Implementation Guide. The data sharing agreement processes are summarized in their own section below. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Personas | Objectives | . | A | Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent | PHW.A | Holder, Consent Recorder, Consent Registry | Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry via [ITI-108] Access Consent (Post, Put, Delete). | . | B | Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link | PHW.B | Holder, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry, Trust Anchor | Register VHL Sharer signing keys with a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record active patient consent ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) stored in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. | . | C | Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement | PHW.C | Holder, VHL Receiver, Trust Anchor, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry | Present a VHL ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic trust via a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY2]), request the manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit / deny / unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with PROV-O provenance. | . Workflows . A. Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent . | Process ID: PHW.A | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn | Objective: Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry using the IHE PCF Access Consent [ITI-108] transaction (Post, Put, Delete), trust-anchor neutral and with no IUA claim. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.A.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Select base policy & disclosure scope (PCF Basic / Intermediate Consent) | Selection of base policy (Consent.policy.uri), PCFPurposeOfUseVS purpose of use, authorized actors, validity period, and clinical data scope | . | PHW.A.2 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Construct FHIR Consent & Provenance (IHE.PCF.consentBasic / Intermediate) | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, IHE.PCF.provenance | . | PHW.A.3 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Create consent directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (POST [base]/Consent or transaction Bundle with Provenance) | . | PHW.A.4 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Update or revoke directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Put / Delete | [ITI-108] Access Consent (PUT [base]/Consent/[id] or DELETE [base]/Consent/[id]) | . | PHW.A.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Validate, version & persist Consent + Provenance [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), assigning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.A.6 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Confirm recorded Consent.id & versionId [ITI-108] Access Consent response | [ITI-108] Access Consent response (201 Created / 200 OK) | . Consent rules, from the person’s side . Process A is the person-side view of the data sharing agreement’s consent process (P9). The owner set four rules on 2026-10-30: . | Legal basis. Only an agreement whose legal basis is consent asks for consent. Treatment, public-health law and research waivers do not rest on consent. | Version pinning. The person consents to one fixed version of the agreement: Consent.policy.uri is that version’s URL. If the agreement is amended to widen use, the new version needs new consent. An amendment that narrows use does not. | Plain language. The person is shown the agreement’s plain-language summary, published and hashed with the agreement. That summary is what they consent to (task PHW.A.1). | Scale. Where the person has recorded nothing, the jurisdiction’s chosen PCF implicit default policy applies: opt-in (for example Policy-deny) or opt-out (for example Policy-basic-normal or Policy-all-normal). Registry lookups may be cached (task PHW.C.5), but withdrawing a Consent (status becomes inactive, task PHW.A.4) ends every cached result that holds it at once. | . B. Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link . | Process ID: PHW.B | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn | Objective: Publish VHL Sharer PKI signing keys to an abstract Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record an active patient privacy consent directive ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) for storage in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others). | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.B.1 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Submit Sharer PKI signing key [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/PublishPKIMaterial) | . | PHW.B.2 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Publish key in Trust Anchor trust list [ITI-YY1] (GDHCN or other anchor) | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/CapabilityStatement/IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.B.3 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Request VHL generation [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL ($generate-vhl) | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/OperationDefinition/GenerateVHL) | . | PHW.B.4 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Query or record active Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search / Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active or POST [base]/Consent) | . | PHW.B.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent (Consent.id + versionId) [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry) | . | PHW.B.5a | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | B5a. Add the consent directives to the shared documents (process M, optional) | Optional (owner, 2026-11-07): before the VHL payload is assembled and signed, process M adds the consent directives the documents are shared under, explicit (the Consent returned at B5) or implied (the trust domain’s default policy), as consent entries listed in each document’s Advance Directives section. The copy in the document is evidence for the receiver; the Consent Registry copy is the one enforced. | . | PHW.B.6 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Assemble & sign VHL payload bound to Consent [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (IHE.VHL.VHLSharer), signing with [ITI-YY1] key material | . | PHW.B.7 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Store signed VHL in Personal Health Wallet [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL response received by VHLHolder | . C. Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement . | Process ID: PHW.C | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn | | Objective: Present a Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic signatures against a Trust Anchor’s trust list ([ITI-YY2]), request the health document manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit | deny | unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with W3C PROV-O decision provenance. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others) and makes no IUA claim. | . | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.C.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Present VHL payload to Receiver [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL | [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/UtilizeVHL) | . | PHW.C.2 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Request Trust Anchor key list [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID | [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/RetrievePKIMaterial) | . | PHW.C.3 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Return signed trust list [ITI-YY2] (GDHCN or other Trust Anchor) | [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID (IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.C.4 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Verify VHL signature & request manifest [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/RequestVHLDocuments) | . | PHW.C.5 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Query active patient Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search | [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active) | . | PHW.C.6 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent Bundle [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), returning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.C.7 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Evaluate PCF Consent (ODRL decide: permit / deny / unknown) & PROV-O log | consentToOdrl() + three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown) + W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.C.8 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Return authorized manifest & documents [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (permit) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (200 OK Bundle of DocumentReference / clinical resources when decision is permit) | . | PHW.C.9 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Refuse disclosure with OperationOutcome [ITI-YY5] (deny or unknown) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (403 Forbidden OperationOutcome when decision is deny or unknown) | . | PHW.C.10 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Process clinical documents or refusal notice [ITI-YY5] response | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest consumer (IHE.VHL.VHLReceiver) | . Data Sharing Agreement Processes (Server to Server) . Processes D to H implement a data sharing agreement (DSA) between a data provider and a data recipient. Each one is a technical process from the DSA process analysis for folio-assistant#2702 (P4, P5, P11, P12 and P13). The owner chose this IG as their home on 2026-10-30 (19:59Z). They apply to every agreement, whether it is computable (a W3C ODRL 2.2 Agreement derived from the legal text) or document-only (a signed PDF). The only difference is where the access rule comes from: the ODRL Agreement, or a configuration an administrator sets by hand from the PDF. What every process relies on: . | The agreement’s fixed-version URL. Each agreement version is published at an immutable URL, with its SHA-256, and catalogued as a DCAT 3 dcat:Distribution with spdx:checksum (DCAT 3 §6.8, §6.8.20). For a computable agreement this URL is also the ODRL uid. Tokens, grants, Consents and audit records cite this URL, never a “latest” URL. | Grants are W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0. A grant cites the agreement through relatedResource (VC DM 2.0 §5.3), and its status is a W3C Bitstring Status List entry. litlfred/smart-trust-tools verifies it. | Pluggable trust anchors. WHO GDHCN is one option. The others are a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list. UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA, is approved (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z) for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication, which fits a national X.509 PKI as the anchor. OpenID Federation is out of scope. | No invented fields. Where no standard has a slot, the text says so as a gap or open point. | . | # | Process Name | Process ID | DSA process | Objectives | . | D | Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.D | P4 | Register the recipient’s server as an OAuth client (RFC 7591, UDAP via HL7 SSRAA, or by an administrator), authenticated by mTLS (RFC 8705) or a JWT assertion (RFC 7523; with UDAP, private_key_jwt with an x5c chain), and record which agreement versions it may act under. | . | E | Server-to-Server Access under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.E | P5 | Issue a short-lived, key-bound token (DPoP, RFC 9449) for an RFC 9396 authorization_details request whose identifier (§2.2) is the agreement’s fixed-version URL, after the access decision. | . | F | Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.F | P11 | Run permits() on the verified grant and the agreement. A consent-based agreement also needs an active PCF Consent. The result is permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. | . | G | Audit, Provenance and Duty Checks under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.G | P12 | Record each decision as a W3C PROV-O record that cites the agreement, and as an IHE ATNA audit event ([ITI-20]). Record duty fulfilment and review it. | . | H | Revocation and Suspension under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.H | P13 | Stop grants (Bitstring Status List), tokens and clients (RFC 7009), and keys (trust list or CRL). | . In the tables, † marks a section number cited from standing knowledge and not re-checked when this page was written. The RFC 9396, RFC 9449, RFC 8693, W3C VC 2.0, W3C Bitstring Status List and DCAT 3 sections were checked against the published specifications on 2026-10-30. D. Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement . | Process ID: PHW.D | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.D.bpmn | Objective: Register the data recipient’s server as an OAuth client of the data provider’s authorization server. It is bound to a key published under a trust anchor the agreement accepts, and to the agreement versions it may act under. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | Standard and section | . | PHW.D.1 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Prepare client key or certificate under an accepted trust anchor | Key published under an accepted anchor (DSA P3): DID Core 1.0 + did:web, or RFC 5280 | . | PHW.D.2 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Send dynamic client registration request (RFC 7591) | RFC 7591 §3.1†; private_key_jwt metadata RFC 7523 §2.2†; tls_client_auth RFC 8705 §2.1†. RFC 7592 is Experimental and needs owner approval | . | PHW.D.3 | Data Provider Administrator (person) | Enter client by hand, scopes from the signed agreement text | Document-only route. The change record cites the agreement URL and its SHA-256 | . | PHW.D.4 | Provider Authorization Server | Validate client key or certificate against the accepted trust anchor | DID document, RFC 5280 §6† path validation, or a local list. UDAP route: UDAP DCR §4‡ (SSRAA §3.2.3): software statement signature, x5c chain to the trust community’s anchor, requested parameters | . | PHW.D.5 | Trust Anchor (GDHCN or another accepted anchor) | Return trust list or certificate status | GDHCN did:web:tng-cdn.who.int:v2:trustlist; CRL RFC 5280 §5† | . | PHW.D.6 | Provider Authorization Server | Record which agreement versions the client may act under | Gap: neither RFC 7591 nor the SSRAA software statement has a field for this, so it is the server’s own configuration. It is keyed by the fixed-version URL, the same value as RFC 9396 identifier (§2.2) | . | PHW.D.7 | Provider Authorization Server | Issue client_id | RFC 7591 §3.2.1†. UDAP route: 201 Created per UDAP DCR §5.1‡, error per §5.2‡ (SSRAA §3.2.3); modify or cancel per SSRAA §3.4 | . | PHW.D.8 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Read authorization server metadata | RFC 8414 §3†. UDAP route: already read in PHW.D.9; token requests use SSRAA §5.2.1–§5.2.2 | . | PHW.D.9 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Discover UDAP server metadata (GET {baseURL}/.well-known/udap) | HL7 SSRAA §2.1, §2.2, §2.3 (signed_metadata), §2.4; UDAP Server Metadata §1‡ | . | PHW.D.10 | Data Recipient System (OAuth client) | Send UDAP registration request with signed software statement | HL7 SSRAA §3.1 (claims; iss = certificate SAN URI; token_endpoint_auth_method = private_key_jwt), §3.2.3 (request body, udap = 1), §3.3 (certifications); UDAP DCR §2‡ | . UDAP route (owner approval, 2026-10-30 20:28Z). UDAP is used as profiled by HL7 Security for Scalable Registration, Authentication, and Authorization (SSRAA), hl7.fhir.us.udap-security 2.0.0 (STU 2, canonical http://hl7.org/fhir/us/udap-security), the IG that VHL’s OAuth with SSRAA Option names. Its trust is X.509: the client’s certificate chains to an anchor of a trust community, so a national X.509 PKI can serve as the anchor without GDHCN. SSRAA section numbers were read from the IG source (HL7/fhir-udap-security-ig, tag 2.0.0, commit d8ac5a63): they follow its page order, and they agree with the IG’s own cross-references, which is also how ITI-YY5 cites them (“SSRAA Sections 2 and 3”, “Section 5.2.1”). The rendered pages at hl7.org were not reachable to check. SSRAA 2.0.0 is US realm; the source’s main branch now builds a universal-realm successor, hl7.fhir.uv.fast-security 3.0.0 (STU 3 post-ballot CI build), not yet published. ‡ marks a section of a UDAP.org specification (UDAP Dynamic Client Registration STU1, UDAP Server Metadata STU1, UDAP JWT-Based Client Authentication STU1) as SSRAA links it; udap.org was not reachable to check it. E. Two more expressions, outside the table, give evaluatedPolicies (every policy) and permittingPolicies (the applicable ones that permitted) for the duties and the audit. Why PRIORITY. The owner’s order (any deny, then any unknown, then any permit, then none applicable) is a ranking of outcomes, and PRIORITY is the DMN hit policy that returns the matching rule whose output comes first in the output’s ordered outputValues. Each rule then states one condition, and the ranking resolves overlaps; for example, a request with a deny and an unknown matches rules 1 and 3, and "deny" wins. Rules with the same output never overlap (rules 1 and 2 differ in conflictStrategy), so the result does not depend on rule order. COLLECT was not used: its aggregators (SUM, MIN, MAX, COUNT) work on numbers, so the outcomes would have to be coded as numbers that no standard defines. FIRST would also work, but it hides the ranking in the rule order. Every combination of up to three policies, with every outcome and strategy, was checked against the owner’s rule, and exactly one outcome results each time. Why only one table. Each row is decided by decide() for that policy alone (PHW.F.10, with the PCF Consent path of PHW.F.8), and applicability is a check of the ODRL target, purpose and assignee. Neither is a decision table, so there is no per-row DMN table. The DMN decision combines the rows once per request. Override 1: the policies. ODRL 2.2 lets each policy declare a conflict strategy with odrl:conflict: odrl:perm (permissions override prohibitions), odrl:prohibit (prohibitions override permissions) or odrl:invalid (the policy is void if any conflict is detected). These terms were checked against the ODRL 2.2 vocabulary and the pinned JSON-LD context (folio-assistant-core scripts/test-fixtures/dsa-contexts/odrl-2.2.context.json). When every applicable policy declares the same strategy, the table uses it. A policy that declares none counts as prohibit, the owner’s default D. If the applicable policies declare different strategies, conflictStrategy is invalid. ODRL 2.2 says a policy with several conflict values (after a merge or inheritance) is void when its rules conflict (W3C ODRL Information Model 2.2, Policy Conflict Strategy). This IG treats the applicable policies of one request as merged. The only declaration that changes an outcome is perm declared by every applicable policy. ODRL’s own default when nothing is declared is invalid, but the outcome is the same: with a conflict, invalid voids the policy and prohibit denies, and both are refused. These two processes are shared blocks for any certificate type (BPMN reuse proposal, Q-BPMN-1 A). A trust domain or another IG calls them instead of copying their steps. Their steps come from the smart-icvp issuing and verifying diagrams. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Objectives | . | J | Issue a Verifiable Digital Health Certificate | PHW.J | Ask the holder for consent, collect what the certificate profile (a data input) needs, issue and sign the certificate, issue its VHL (process B), and deliver it to the wallet. | . | K | Verify a Certificate and its Status | PHW.K | Receive the claim; redeem a VHL through process C, check by hand, or decode the QR code, get the issuer key from the Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY2]), verify the signature, and check the registry. | . J. Issue a Verifiable Digital Health Certificate . | Process ID: PHW.J | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.J.bpmn | Objective: Shared block B4 of the BPMN reuse proposal (Q-BPMN-1 A, 2026-11-01): one issuing process for every certificate type. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | Source | . | PHW.J.1 | Certificate Issuer (health worker or issuing system) | J1. Inform the holder and ask for consent to issue | smart-icvp: ‘Inform traveller and request consent to digitize’ and ‘Counsel patient on consent’. This is consent to issue the certificate. Consent to share it later is recorded by process A and checked by process B. | . | PHW.J.2 | Certificate Issuer (health worker or issuing system) | J2. Collect the data the certificate profile needs | smart-icvp: ‘Capture Vaccination Data’, ‘Collate ICVP data’, ‘Conduct data entry from physical card into system’. What is collected is set by the certificate profile input. | . | PHW.J.2a | Certificate Issuance Service | J2a. Add the consent directives to the certificate (process M, optional) | Optional (owner, 2026-11-07): before the certificate is signed, process M adds the consent directives it is issued under, explicit (PHWExplicitConsent, recorded by process L) or implied (PHWImpliedConsent, the trust domain’s default policy), as consent entries listed in the Advance Directives section. The copy in the certificate is evidence for a receiver; the Consent Registry copy is the one enforced. | . | PHW.J.3 | Certificate Issuance Service | J3. Issue and sign the certificate | smart-icvp: ‘Issue Digital ICVP Card’. Signed with the issuer’s key registered with the trust anchor. | . | PHW.J.4 | Certificate Issuance Service | J4. Issue a consent-backed VHL (process B) | smart-icvp: ‘Configure VHL’. Reuses process B: consent check [ITI-108] and Generate VHL [ITI-YY3]. | . | PHW.J.5 | Certificate Issuance Service | J5. Generate the QR code | smart-icvp: ‘Generate QR Code’. | . | PHW.J.6 | Certificate Holder (person / Personal Health Wallet) | J6. Receive the certificate in the wallet | smart-icvp: ‘Receive Digital ICVP Card’, ‘Digital ICVP Card issued and available for use’. | . K. Verify a Certificate and its Status . | Process ID: PHW.K | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.K.bpmn | Objective: Shared block B7 of the BPMN reuse proposal (Q-BPMN-1 A, 2026-11-01): one verifying process for every certificate type. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | Source | . | PHW.K.1 | Verifier (with or without a status checking application) | K1. Receive the claim | smart-icvp: ‘Receive claim of vaccination status’. | . | PHW.K.VHL | Certificate Holder (person / Personal Health Wallet) | K2. Present and redeem the VHL (process C) | Reuses process C: [ITI-YY4], [ITI-YY2], [ITI-YY5] with consent enforcement. | . | PHW.K.Manual | Verifier (with or without a status checking application) | K3. Check by hand and decide the claim | smart-icvp: ‘Perform Manual Check and decide the status of the claim’. Done by the Verifier when no checking application is used. | . | PHW.K.4 | Verifier (with or without a status checking application) | K4. Decode the QR code and find the key id | smart-icvp: ‘Deserialize the QR Code and identify the Key Id’. | . | PHW.K.5 | Trust Anchor (GDHCN or another accepted anchor) | K5. Return the issuer’s public key [ITI-YY2] | smart-icvp: ‘Retrieve public key from WHO GDHCN’. [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID. | . | PHW.K.6 | Verifier (with or without a status checking application) | K6. Verify the signature and the claim | smart-icvp: ‘Verify QR code signature’ and ‘Verify Certificate claim’. | . | PHW.K.7 | Issuing Public Health Authority (certificate registry) | K7. Find the certificate in the registry and return it | smart-icvp: ‘Identify Certificate in Certificate Registry’, ‘Retrieve Certificate from Certificate Repository’, ‘Return Certificate’. | . | PHW.K.8 | Verifier (with or without a status checking application) | K8. Communicate the result | smart-icvp: ‘Communicate Result back to Verifier’. | . Consent Processes . Explicit and implied consent are described on the Consent page. Process L records an explicit consent. Process M adds the consent directives, explicit or implied, to a document when it is shared (process B, step B5a) or issued (process J, step J2a). Adding them is optional. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Objectives | . | L | Record Explicit Consent | PHW.L | Show the trust domain’s consent text (code and version); when the holder agrees, record the act as evidence and post a PHWExplicitConsent with [ITI-108]; when the holder does not, the trust domain’s default policy applies (implied consent). | . | M | Add Consent Directives to a Shared or Issued Document | PHW.M | Optionally, before signing: find the active explicit Consents ([ITI-108]), or else the trust domain’s default as a PHWImpliedConsent; add them as consent entries and list them in the Advance Directives section. | . Show the trust domain’s consent text (code and version) | The text is the definition of the consent code in the trust domain’s terms-of-use code system, at the version shown, in the holder’s language. For Hajj: IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT, for example CONSENT-MYS at 2.1.0. | . | PHW.L.2 | Holder (person / Personal Health Wallet) | L2. Read the text and decide | The holder decides who may see what, for what purpose and for how long (provision.actor, provision.purpose, provision.period). | . | PHW.L.3 | PCF Consent Recorder (wallet or health worker) | L3. Record the holder’s act as evidence | The wallet confirmation or the signed form (a DocumentReference or QuestionnaireResponse): the Consent’s source[x]. | . | PHW.L.4 | PCF Consent Recorder (wallet or health worker) | L4. Post the explicit Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent | A PHWExplicitConsent: policyRule = the trust domain’s consent code with the version shown; source = the evidence of L3; status active. | . | PHW.L.5 | PCF Consent Registry | L5. Store the Consent; return Consent.id and versionId [ITI-108] | The registry copy is the one enforced (processes C, F, I). | . | PHW.L.6 | Holder (person / Personal Health Wallet) | L6. Keep a copy in the wallet | So the holder can read back what they agreed to and withdraw it (process A, Delete or Put). | . M. Add Consent Directives to a Shared or Issued Document . | Process ID: PHW.M | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.M.bpmn | Objective: A shared or issued document can carry the consent directives it is shared under, explicit or implied, so the receiver can see them. The copy in the document is evidence; the Consent Registry copy is the one enforced. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | Description | . | PHW.M.1 | Document source (VHL Sharer or Certificate Issuance Service) | M1. Search active Consents for the holder [ITI-108] Access Consent | Explicit consents for this trust domain: policyRule in the domain’s terms-of-use ValueSet. | . | PHW.M.2 | PCF Consent Registry | M2. Return the active Consents [ITI-108] | With Consent.id and meta.versionId. | . | PHW.M.3 | Document source (VHL Sharer or Certificate Issuance Service) | M3. 756f1f40d2ef.title: Consent
756f1f40d2ef.content: . This page describes how a Personal Health Wallet handles consent. Consent follows IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0. Each trust domain sets the consent policies that apply in it. The processes on this page are trust-anchor neutral: GDHCN is one possible trust anchor among others. Two kinds of consent . Each consent records its kind in Consent.category with a code from HL7 v3 ActConsentDirective (CodeSystem v3-ActCode). HL7 defines every one of these codes; this guide adds none. |   | Explicit consent | Implied consent | . | What it is | The holder agrees, or refuses, by their own act: on their wallet, or on a form a health worker records. | The holder does nothing. The trust domain’s default policy applies. | . | Kind (Consent.category, HL7 ActConsentDirective) | OPTIN (opt-in), OPTINR (opt-in with restrictions), OPTOUT (opt-out), OPTOUTE (opt-out with exceptions): PHW Explicit Consent Kind | IMPLIED (implied consent), IMPLIEDD (implied consent with opportunity to dissent), NOPP (notice of privacy practices): PHW Implied Consent Kind | . | How it is recorded | A PHW Explicit Consent in the Consent Registry (process L, IHE PCF [ITI-108]). | Not recorded per holder. A document may carry it as a PHW Implied Consent. | . | The policy | Consent.policyRule: the trust domain’s consent code with its version, when the domain publishes consent codes. Otherwise Consent.policy.uri: the IHE PCF implicit policy the consent changes. | Consent.policy.uri: the trust domain’s default policy, normally an IHE PCF implicit policy (Policy-basic-normal, Policy-all-normal, Policy-break-glass-only or Policy-deny). | . | The evidence (Consent.source[x]) | The holder’s recorded act: the wallet confirmation or the signed form. | The trust domain’s published policy. | . | State | Consent.status (FHIR R4): proposed, active, rejected, inactive (withdrawn or expired), entered-in-error. | The same. | . IHE PCF does not allow Consent.verification, so the kind is carried in category. Both kinds are IHE PCF Intermediate Consents (PHW Consent). An opt-in trust domain has Policy-deny as its default, so data is shared only with explicit consent. An opt-out trust domain has Policy-basic-normal or Policy-all-normal as its default, so data is shared unless the holder dissents. The kind and ODRL . Consent is decided by translating it to W3C ODRL 2.2 (consentToOdrl() in fhir-harness), where each IHE PCF implicit policy is an ODRL Set. The kind says which of those Sets a consent builds on, through ODRL’s inheritFrom: . | Kind | Builds on (odrl:inheritFrom) | What the consent adds | . | OPTIN, OPTINR | Policy-deny | Its permissions (OPTINR: with the holder’s restrictions as prohibitions or constraints) | . | OPTOUT | Policy-deny | Nothing: the holder refuses | . | OPTOUTE | Policy-basic-normal | Its prohibitions, with the holder’s exceptions as permissions | . | IMPLIED, IMPLIEDD, NOPP | Its own Consent.policy | Nothing: the implied consent is its policy’s Set | . So a receiver, or the Sharer’s decision point, can tell from the code alone what holds when no permission matches. Reading category this way is a proposed change to consentToOdrl(), which today reads policy and policyRule only. Trust domains and their consent codes . A trust domain may name its own consent policies as a terms-of-use ValueSet (TrustDomain.termsOfUse in the GDHCN Trust IG). Each code’s definition is the text the holder is shown. An explicit consent names one of these codes in policyRule. A VHL Receiver’s credential names one in its termsOfUse (see process I). The Sharer finds the trust domain from the ValueSet that holds the code. For the IPS Pilgrimage trust domain, the codes are IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT in the IPS Pilgrimage guide, for example CONSENT-MYS and CONSENT-KSA. The worked example shows the two Hajj consents as PilgrimConsentOriginRelease and PilgrimConsentHostUse. Consent directives in shared and issued documents . A document that is shared or issued may carry the consent directives it is shared under, explicit or implied. Carrying them is optional: the trust domain, or the holder in the wallet, decides. Process M adds them before the document is signed. Process B calls it at step B5a and process J at step J2a. | Each directive is a consent entry of the document Bundle (IPS document that carries its consent directives). | The Composition’s Advance Directives section (LOINC 42348-3) lists them, with a summary that a person can read. | The copy in the document is evidence. The sharer enforces the copy in its own Consent Registry. A signed document cannot show a later withdrawal. | . LinaSummaryWithConsent is an example. Lina’s patient summary carries her explicit consent, an OPTIN (LinaExplicitConsent), and the trust domain’s default, an IMPLIEDD under Policy-basic-normal (LinaImpliedConsent). Every person in the examples is fictional. Deciding access . When a link is redeemed (process C) or a request comes under an agreement (processes F and I), the sharer reads the active Consents from its registry with [ITI-108]. It translates them to W3C ODRL 2.2 and decides permit, deny or unknown. A missing, expired or unreachable consent never gives permit. The decision is recorded as W3C PROV-O provenance that cites Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. Edit this page on GitHub .

d6d2201ac36b.title: Worked Example: IPS Pilgrimage (Hajj)
d6d2201ac36b.content: . This page is a worked example. It applies the business processes A, B, C, F and I of this guide to one case: the IPS Pilgrimage (Hajj) implementation guide (smart-ips-pilgrimage, FHIR R4, IHE PCF 1.1.0). It follows the analysis written for folio-assistant#2702 on 2026-10-30. The case: during Hajj, the host country (KSA) is the VHL Receiver. It asks the pilgrim’s origin country (for example Malaysia) for the pilgrim’s International Patient Summary (IPS) over a Verifiable Health Link (VHL). The origin country’s health information exchange (HIE) is the VHL Sharer. The IPS carries two consent statements from the pilgrim, and those two Consents are the policy for the exchange. The page does not change the IPS Pilgrimage guide. The gaps below say what that guide, or the specifications it uses, would need. Gap G1 has since been resolved in that guide by smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. The pilgrim’s consents are the policy . For Hajj, there is no separate data sharing agreement for the Sharer to look up. The pilgrim’s two Consents are the policy, and each is coded in Consent.policyRule (owner, Q-DRAIN-5, 2026-11-01 07:44Z). That is how the IPS Pilgrimage guide models them since smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. policyRule holds a code from that guide’s IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT CodeSystem, with coding.version set to the CodeSystem version whose consent text the pilgrim was shown. Any arrangement between KSA and the origin country, such as a memorandum of understanding, stays outside the computable decision. Each Consent binds the party it names: . | Consent | What it allows | Who is bound, and where it is checked | . | Origin release (CONSENT-<origin>, for example CONSENT-MYS) | The origin HIE may release the IPS to the KSA Ministry of Health, as information recipient, for treatment, during the Hajj period. | The origin HIE. It enforces this Consent from its own Consent Registry ([ITI-108]) at step 10. The Consent’s decide() result is one row of the default DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (PHW.F.10). | . | Host use (CONSENT-KSA) | The KSA Ministry of Health may use the IPS for care during Hajj and any follow-up. | KSA, which follows it after receipt (step 14). The origin does not enforce it. | . The receiver is identified by trust: its key or certificate is accepted in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain (PHW.I.2, PHW.I.3). There is no agreement lookup at PHW.I.4. “Patient-mediated” then means three things, each an existing mechanism: . | The pilgrim records the consents (PCF [ITI-108], process A). | The pilgrim carries the link (the VHL QR code, [ITI-YY4], process C). | The pilgrim is present at the encounter. Giving the passcode (the VHL P flag; ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.5.8) is the in-person act. | . The registry copy is enforced; the IPS copy is evidence. The IPS Bundle also carries copies of both Consents. They travel with the data as evidence for KSA. The Sharer does not enforce them: it enforces the copy in its own Consent Registry. The IPS is signed once, when it is issued, so its copy cannot show a later withdrawal (consent rule 4). The flow, step by step . The Hajj encounter, mapped onto VHL and onto the activities of this guide. Steps that hit a gap name it; the gaps are listed in the next section. Before Hajj . | # | Step | Actor | PHW activities | Transaction | Gap | . | 1 | Trust. The origin HIE publishes its signing keys to the ips-pilgrimage trust domain. GDHCN is the trust anchor here, as one option among others. KSA must also publish its own keys or certificates there, so that the origin can authenticate it at step 9. | Origin HIE, Trust Anchor | PHW.B.1, PHW.B.2 | [ITI-YY1] | G3 | . | 2 | Registration. With the OAuth with SSRAA option, KSA’s EMR registers with the origin HIE by UDAP (HL7 SSRAA), using a certificate that chains to an anchor of the ips-pilgrimage trust domain. With HTTP Message Signatures, nothing is registered: the origin reads KSA’s key from the trust list. No agreement URL is involved. | Origin HIE, KSA EMR | PHW.D.9, PHW.D.10 | — | G3 | . | 3 | Counselling and consent. A counsellor explains the plain-language text of each consent (consent rule 3). The wallet records both Consents in the origin’s Consent Registry. Each Consent’s policyRule names which Hajj consent it is (CONSENT-<origin> or CONSENT-KSA), and its coding.version names the IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT version whose text the pilgrim was shown. The link’s expiry should not run past the Consents’ provision.period. | Pilgrim, Origin HIE | PHW.B.3, PHW.B.4, PHW.B.5, PHW.B.6, PHW.B.7 | [ITI-YY3], [ITI-108] |   | . At the encounter in KSA . | # | Step | Actor | PHW activities | Transaction | Gap | . | 6 | The pilgrim shows the QR code and gives the passcode. | Pilgrim | PHW.C.1 | [ITI-YY4] |   | . | 7 | The KSA EMR verifies the HCERT/CWT signature against the trust list. | KSA EMR, Trust Anchor | PHW.C.2, PHW.C.3, PHW.C.4 | [ITI-YY2] |   | . | 8 | The KSA EMR registers the pilgrim with the pilgrimage number. | KSA EMR | — (IPS Pilgrimage guide, step 03) | — |   | . | 9 | The KSA EMR sends Retrieve Manifest with the passcode, authenticated by one VHL option. The IPS Pilgrimage guide uses mTLS node authentication ([ITI-19]) today, which is not one of VHL’s options. | KSA EMR | PHW.I.1 | [ITI-YY5] | G3, G4, G5 | . | 10 | The origin HIE decides. (a) It authenticates KSA by trust in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain. There is no agreement lookup: the Consents are the policy. (b) It searches its own registry for the pilgrim’s active origin-release Consent (policyRule = CONSENT-<origin>). (c) It evaluates that Consent with decide() (see the conditions below). The result is the Consent’s row in the default DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess, whose outcome routes the request. (d) Anything missing gives unknown, and unknown is never permit. | Origin HIE, Consent Registry | (a) PHW.I.2, PHW.I.3; (b) PHW.I.5 → PHW.F.8, PHW.F.9; (c) PHW.F.10; (d) PHW.F.11, PHW.I.6 or PHW.I.7 | [ITI-YY5], [ITI-YY2], [ITI-108] | G2 | . | 11 | Audit. The origin HIE records an audit event. It cites the governing Consents by policyRule code and CodeSystem version, the id and meta.versionId of each Consent read for the decision, which of them permitted, the DMN decision used, the receiver, the purpose, and the documents released or the refusal. | Origin HIE, writing to the Audit Record Repository | PHW.I.9 (with PHW.G.1) | [ITI-20] |   | . | 12 | The origin HIE returns the List and its DocumentReferences (_include=List:item, VHL’s Include DocumentReference Option), then the IPS. | Origin HIE | PHW.I.6 | [ITI-YY5], [ITI-68] |   | . | 13 | The KSA EMR verifies the IPS signature, stores a copy and shows it. | KSA EMR | PHW.I.11 | — |   | . | 14 | KSA follows CONSENT-KSA after receipt. Nothing machine-readable travels with the document to say so yet. | KSA Ministry of Health | process G (PHW.G.5, PHW.G.6) | — | G6 | . When does step 10 permit? Only when every one of these holds: . | the passcode is valid; | the link has not expired; | the origin-release Consent is active in the origin’s own registry; | the KSA Ministry of Health, as verified by trust in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain, is the consented actor (provision.actor); | the purpose is treatment (provision.purpose = TREAT); | today is inside the Hajj period (provision.period). | . The origin-release Consent is found by its policyRule code (CONSENT-<origin>), and its coding.version names the consent text the pilgrim was shown. The KSA-use Consent binds KSA, not the origin, so the origin does not need it to permit. With only one Consent applicable, the default DMN decision returns that Consent’s own result. Gaps . Ordered by how much each one blocks a computable decision. Each row names the existing standard that would close it. Nothing here invents a field. | Gap | What is missing | What would close it | . | G1. The Hajj consents are not computable as written. Resolved by smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. | Was: the consent type sat in provision.purpose, the examples had display names only, and policyRule.text was "some policy", so decide() would return unknown every time. Still open in that guide: the consent texts for two origin countries (CONSENT-IDN, CONSENT-OMN) are placeholders (consent rule 3). | HajjConsent now requires policyRule with an IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT code and coding.version (CodeSystem version 2.1.0). policyRule also satisfies R4 invariant ppc-1, so no policy.uri is needed. It also requires provision.actor (an Organization by identifier, role IRCP), provision.purpose from v3 PurposeOfUse (TREAT), and provision.period. See the examples below. | . | G2. Which copy of a consent counts. | The specifications do not say whether the Sharer enforces the registry copy or the copy inside the IPS, or what KSA should do with its copy. | A rule in the implementation guide, not a new field: the Sharer enforces the registry copy (PCF [ITI-108]); the IPS copy is evidence, carrying its meta.versionId so that KSA can cite it. | . | G3. mTLS is not a VHL option. | The IPS Pilgrimage guide’s sequence diagram still authenticates the KSA node with mTLS ([ITI-19]). Since smart-ips-pilgrimage#3, its transaction page says that mTLS is not one of VHL [ITI-YY5]’s three options and recommends OAuth with SSRAA. How KSA’s certificate or key is published in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain is still not specified. | Choose one VHL option: OAuth with SSRAA (UDAP), approved for process D and I, which is X.509-based like mTLS; or HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). KSA publishes the matching key in the trust domain ([ITI-YY1]). | . | G4. The facility and the clinician are invisible. | CONSENT-KSA is limited to healthcare facilities in the Hajj district, but the request comes from one national KSA EMR. With HTTP Message Signatures, the Sharer sees only KSA, so it cannot check the district limit and the audit cannot name who looked. | HL7 SSRAA: the hl7-b2b extension carries organization_id and the requesting user (SSRAA §5.2.1.1). | . | G5. The purpose of use is not carried. | [ITI-YY5] has no purpose parameter, so the decision assumes TREAT from the Consent’s provision.purpose. This is open point 3 of process I. | HL7 SSRAA purpose_of_use in hl7-b2b (SSRAA §5.2.1.1), with HL7 v3 PurposeOfUse codes. | . | G6. KSA’s duties after receipt are not machine-readable. | CONSENT-KSA allows “any follow up care” and says nothing about retention or onward sharing. Nothing in VHL, IPS or PCF carries such obligations with the document. | Either HL7 Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) obligation codes in meta.security (needs owner approval: not final), or, with approved standards only, KSA keeps following the CONSENT-KSA text it is bound by and audits against it in process G, with no labels on the document. | . | G7. What the audit event cites. Resolved by smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. | Was: the IPS Pilgrimage guide had [ITI-20] at the origin HIE but did not say what the event contains. | That guide now states it, as process I gives it (PHW.I.9): the Consents by policyRule code and CodeSystem version, each Consent’s id and meta.versionId, receiver, purpose and documents released or the refusal. KSA, as an ATNA Secure Node (VHL Vol 1 §1:XX.3), also audits what it receives. IHE BALP patterns need owner approval. | . | G8. Break the glass has no VHL. | In phase 2 of the IPS Pilgrimage guide (process 5.0) the pilgrim may be unconscious: no QR code and no passcode, so the lookup is by pilgrimage number, outside VHL entirely. | Its own search transaction (likely IHE PDQm [ITI-78] with IHE MHD [ITI-67]), a separate opt-in Consent (the wallet’s “break the glass” setting), and the emergency purpose of use ETREAT. Not specified today. | . | G9. Versions and status. | The IPS Pilgrimage guide does not depend on VHL. It describes the VHL steps in its own transaction pages, partly in older SMART Health Links wording (“modified ITI-67”). Its HajjConsent notes on FHIR R5 (verification.verifiedBy, Consent.period) are for later. | Depend on IHE VHL and cite it as what it is: 1.0.0-comment, a public-comment ballot. The guide’s _include=List:item already matches VHL’s Include DocumentReference Option. FHIR R4 with PCF 1.1.0 already matches the approved PCF version. | . Example consents . The two Consents below match the HajjConsent examples of smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. They are FHIR R4 resources on the IHE PCF 1.1.0 profile IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, which HajjConsent is built on. This guide is built on FHIR R4 4.0.1 too, and the two are instances of its PHW Explicit Consent profile: each names a Hajj consent code in policyRule and has the consent text the pilgrim was shown as its evidence. Every name, identifier, URL and date is a fictional example: . | The pilgrim, the Malaysian HIE and the Saudi Ministry of Health are stand-ins, as in smart-ips-pilgrimage#3. Their identifiers are example.org URLs. | 2025-05-01 to 2025-08-31 stands in for the Hajj period (Hajj 1446/2025, as the IPS.HAJJ.CONSENT 2.1.0 text says), with time for follow-up care. | . Both Consents permit the same recipient, for the same purpose and period. They differ in which Hajj consent they are (policyRule), and so in the text the pilgrim was shown (sourceAttachment) and in whom they bind: the first lets the origin release the IPS, and the second lets the host use it. Only existing elements are used: policyRule (with coding.version), provision.actor, provision.purpose and provision.period. There is no policy.uri, because there is no separate agreement. The instances are in this guide’s artefacts: PilgrimConsentOriginRelease and PilgrimConsentHostUse, both PHW Explicit Consent, with the pilgrim, the origin HIE and the host Ministry of Health. How step 10 reads them: the origin HIE takes the active Consent whose policyRule is its own release code (CONSENT-MYS) from its registry (PHW.F.8). It matches provision.actor.reference.identifier against the receiver as verified by trust in the ips-pilgrimage trust domain (PHW.I.2), provision.purpose against the purpose (TREAT; see G5), and provision.period against today. That Consent’s decide() result feeds the default DMN decision PHW.DT.AgreementAccess (PHW.F.10). PilgrimConsentHostUse (CONSENT-KSA) binds the host Ministry of Health after receipt and is not part of the origin’s decision. The audit event (PHW.I.9) cites each Consent read, by policyRule code and version and by the id and meta.versionId the registry assigned at PHW.A.5. Open questions for the owner . | G6: approve DS4P obligation codes, or keep KSA’s duties in the CONSENT-KSA text only? | G8: is break the glass in scope now? | . Edit this page on GitHub .

4c95635c6dd9.content: The reference for folio-assistant-core/library/arxiv-2510.21603v1 (folio-assistant-core, a dependency of smart-trust-phw) and any references extracted from it. folio-assistant-core-library · All references. Dong∗, Kuicai; Huang∗, Shurui; Ye∗, Fangda; et al.. Doc-Researcher: A Unified System for Multimodal Document Parsing and Deep Research. TitleDoc-Researcher: A Unified System for Multimodal Document Parsing and Deep Research AuthorsDong∗, Kuicai; Huang∗, Shurui; Ye∗, Fangda; Han, Wei; Zhang, Zhi; Li, Dexun; Li, Wenjun; Yang, Qu IssuedD:20251027 Typearticle-journal NotearXiv:2510.21603 AbstractDeep Research systems have revolutionized how LLMs solve com- plex questions through iterative reasoning and evidence gathering. However, current systems remain fundamentally constrained to textual web data, overlooking the vast knowledge embedded in mul- timodal documents: scientific papers, technical reports, and finan- cial documents where critical information exists in figures, tables, charts, and equations. Processing such documents demands sophis- ticated parsing to preserve visual semantics, intelligent chunking to maintain structural coherence, and adaptive retrieval across modal- ities, which are capabilities absent in existing systems. In response, we present Doc-Researcher, a unified system that bridges this gap through three integrated components: (i) deep multimodal parsing that preserves layout structure and visual semantics while creating multi-granular representations from chunk to document level, (ii) systematic retrieval architecture supporting text-only, vision-only, and hybrid paradigms with dynamic granularity selec- tion, and (iii) iterative multi-agent workflows that decompose complex queries, progressively accumulate evidence, and synthesize comprehensive answers across documents and modalities. To enable rigorous evaluation, we introduce M4DocBench, the first bench- mark for Multi-modal, Multi-hop, Multi-document, and Multi-turn deep research. Featuring 158 expert-annotated questions with com- plete evidence chains across 304 documents, M4DocBench tests capabilities that existing benchmarks cannot assess. Experiments demonstrate that Doc-Researcher achieves 50.6% accuracy, 3.4× better than state-of-the-art baselines, validating that effective docu- ment research requires not just better retrieval, but fundamentally deep parsing that preserve multimodal integrity and support itera- tive research. Our work establishes a new paradigm for conducting deep research on multimodal document collections. f9df60a96f8a.content: World Health Organization (2016). WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience. World Health Organization. TitleWHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2016-11-7 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241549912 Languageen AbstractThis guideline presents the World Health Organization’s evidence-based recommendations on routine antenatal care to support a positive pregnancy experience for pregnant women and adolescent girls. It aims to provide a comprehensive, consolidated framework for antenatal care that complements existing WHO guidance on the management of specific pregnancy-related complications. The recommendations promote a person-centred, rights-based approach that extends beyond the prevention of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality to enhance women’s physical, psychological and sociocultural well-being, support healthy pregnancies, and improve the quality and utilization of antenatal care. Intended for policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals, the guideline informs the development of national policies, clinical protocols and service delivery models. Developed according to the WHO guideline development process, the document draws on systematic reviews and applies the GRADE and GRADE-CERQual approaches together with the DECIDE evidence-to-decision framework. It contains 49 recommendations covering nutritional interventions, maternal and fetal assessment, preventive measures, management of common physiological symptoms, and health system interventions to improve antenatal care utilization and quality. The guideline also introduces the 2016 WHO antenatal care model, recommending a minimum of eight contacts during pregnancy, and emphasizes implementation, dissemination and periodic updating as new evidence becomes available. c78db8d85431.content: World Health Organization (2024). Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture. World Health Organization. TitleDigital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-11-11 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240101197 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides practical guidance for countries seeking to digitally transform public health supply chains through the development of coherent strategies, interoperable architectures and sustainable implementation approaches. Developed within the WHO SMART Guidelines framework, it addresses the growing need for integrated digital ecosystems that support forecasting, procurement, warehousing, distribution, dispensing and traceability of health products. The publication outlines the role of digital technologies in improving efficiency, data availability, interoperability and decision-making across supply chain processes, while helping ensure timely access to quality-assured medicines and health products. The publication presents a stepwise approach for defining a digital health supply chain (DHSC) strategy, assessing existing health supply chain information systems, designing a target architecture, planning implementation and supporting product traceability. It emphasizes stakeholder engagement, alignment with national health, digital health and supply chain strategies, use of open standards, and long-term scalability and sustainability. Drawing on country experiences and established digital health frameworks, the handbook offers practical tools, templates and examples to support governance, planning and coordination of digital transformation initiatives, with the aim of strengthening supply chain performance, improving visibility across the supply chain and enhancing patient safety. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and monitoring: recommendations for a public health approach AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2021-7-16 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240031593 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThese consolidated guidelines provide comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations for HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery and programme monitoring across the continuum of HIV care. Updating the 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines, this edition integrates guidance issued between 2016 and 2021 and reflects major advances in clinical practice, diagnostics and service delivery. Developed using the GRADE approach and informed by expert consultation and country experience, the guidelines aim to support countries in implementing high-quality, person-centred HIV services while advancing universal health coverage and progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. The publication addresses HIV testing strategies, prevention interventions, antiretroviral therapy, management of advanced HIV disease, care for common coinfections and comorbidities, differentiated service delivery, procurement, laboratory services and programme monitoring. It incorporates updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis, dolutegravir-based treatment, rapid antiretroviral therapy initiation, viral load monitoring and community-based models of care. Intended primarily for national HIV programme managers, policy-makers and health-care providers, the guidelines also serve as a resource for technical partners, community organizations and people living with HIV to support the implementation of effective, equitable and people-centred HIV programmes. TitleDigital adaptation kit for immunizations: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2024-12-31 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240099456 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis publication presents the World Health Organization’s digital adaptation kit (DAK) for immunizations, developed within the SMART Guidelines framework to support the implementation of WHO immunization recommendations in digital systems. The document provides operational and software-neutral specifications intended to facilitate the translation of immunization guidance into interoperable digital health applications, particularly person-centred point-of-service systems and electronic immunization registries. It outlines the role of digital adaptation kits in strengthening digital health systems by improving the consistency, transparency and standardization of health content, workflows, data structures and decision-support logic used in immunization programmes. The publication also situates the DAK within broader digital health strategies and interoperability standards. The document describes eight core components of the immunization DAK, including health interventions and recommendations, generic personas, user scenarios, workflows, core data elements, decision-support logic, indicators and functional requirements. It incorporates WHO guidance related to routine immunization, electronic immunization registries and digital health interventions, while emphasizing adaptability to country-specific policies and implementation contexts. Additional sections address interoperability, data standards, workflow optimization and the use of digital systems to support longitudinal tracking, reporting, decision support and communication within immunization services. The publication is intended for immunization programme managers, digital health teams, software developers and implementers involved in designing and deploying digital immunization systems. TitleDigital transformation handbook for health product catalogue AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2025-10-30 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractThis handbook provides guidance for the implementation of standardized product master data management through national product catalogues (NPCs) to support digital transformation in health supply chains. Developed within the framework of the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide and aligned with the SMART Guidelines initiative, the publication outlines regulatory, governance, technological and operational approaches for establishing interoperable product registries and harmonized product information systems. It explains the importance of standardized product master data for ensuring accurate identification, tracking and management of health products across manufacturers, regulatory authorities, procurement entities, warehouses, health facilities and other supply chain stakeholders. The handbook describes policies and procedures for data governance, coding structures, interoperability standards, change management and capacity-building to support sustainable implementation. It also presents guidance on integrating standardized product master data with digital health, regulatory and supply chain systems to improve forecasting, procurement, inventory management, pharmacovigilance, product recalls and traceability. In addition, the publication highlights mechanisms for sharing product master data as a global good and leveraging WHO-hosted tools and open standards to strengthen coordination, data quality and supply chain efficiency across countries and organizations. TitleNational health workforce accounts: health workforce levels and trends 2026 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-6-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240122925 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis report presents the 2026 edition of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) series, providing an overview of the status of NHWA implementation and an analysis of global and regional health workforce levels and trends based on official data reported by countries to the World Health Organization. Developed to support evidence-informed health workforce policy-making and planning, the report examines progress in strengthening national health workforce information systems, data availability and reporting across countries, and the use of standardized indicators to monitor human resources for health in support of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals and other health objectives. Drawing on the 2025 NHWA data release, the report analyses the distribution, density and composition of the health and care workforce across regions and income groups, highlighting persistent disparities in workforce availability. It also examines trends in workforce growth since 2006 and presents a thematic analysis of population ageing and health workforce ageing, assessing their implications for future workforce needs. The findings demonstrate substantial improvements in the availability and quality of health workforce data through NHWA implementation while underscoring continuing challenges related to workforce shortages, inequities in distribution and the need for sustained investment in health workforce planning and monitoring. TitleConsolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, 2019 AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2020-11-3 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241550581 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis guideline provides comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations to support countries in delivering high-quality, person-centred HIV testing services (HTS) across diverse populations and settings. Updating and consolidating previous WHO guidance issued in 2015 and 2016, it incorporates new evidence on HIV self-testing, social network-based HIV testing approaches, western blotting, and strategic service delivery to strengthen progress towards global HIV targets. Developed using the GRADE methodology and informed by systematic reviews, modelling studies and expert consultation, the guideline aims to improve the effectiveness, efficiency and quality of HIV testing while promoting timely linkage to prevention, treatment and care. The publication addresses the full continuum of HIV testing services, including demand creation, pre- and post-test services, facility- and community-based testing, implementation considerations for priority populations, strategic planning, diagnostic testing strategies, quality assurance and programme monitoring. It provides updated recommendations on HIV self-testing, provider-assisted referral, social network-based approaches and the use of dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests, while emphasizing the WHO 5Cs of HIV testing services: consent, confidentiality, counselling, correct results and connection. Intended for policy-makers, national programme managers, health-care providers and implementing partners, the guideline supports the expansion of equitable, evidence-informed HIV testing services to improve diagnosis and strengthen national HIV responses. 664e0653055a.doc: National health workforce accounts: implementation guide
664e0653055a.title: National health workforce accounts: implementation guide
664e0653055a.content: World Health Organization (2018). National health workforce accounts: implementation guide. World Health Organization. TitleNational health workforce accounts: implementation guide AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2018-10-19 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789241514446 Languageen AbstractThe National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) Implementation Guide provides practical guidance for countries on establishing and sustaining systems to collect, analyse, use and report standardized health workforce data. Developed as a companion document to the NHWA Handbook and in support of the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, the guide outlines a structured approach to strengthening health workforce information systems and improving the availability, quality and use of human resources for health data. It is intended for policy-makers, programme managers, technical experts and stakeholders involved in health workforce planning, monitoring and governance, and emphasizes collaboration across sectors such as health, education, labour, finance and statistics. The guide presents an implementation framework organized into three phases—conceptualization, operationalization, and scaling up and sustainability—comprising eight steps that address political commitment, governance arrangements, planning, legal considerations, data compilation and analysis, validation, dissemination, and process review. It describes the roles of national institutions and multistakeholder coordination mechanisms, provides guidance on data quality, reporting and communication processes, and promotes the integration of existing information systems. By supporting the systematic monitoring of health workforce indicators, the guide aims to strengthen evidence-informed decision-making and contribute to health workforce development, universal health coverage and broader national and global health objectives. ee25150a1c33.title: Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses …
ee25150a1c33.content: World Health Organization (2023). Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health. World Health Organization. TitleClassification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-10-24 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240081949 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health provides a standardized taxonomy for describing how digital technologies are used to address individual and health system needs. Developed by WHO, the classification establishes a shared language to support communication among policy-makers, health programme managers, researchers, implementers, technology developers and other stakeholders involved in digital health. It organizes digital health interventions around discrete technological capabilities designed to address health system challenges and links these interventions to the digital services and application types through which they are delivered. The publication updates and expands the first edition published in 2018 to reflect advances in digital health technologies, evolving implementation practices and lessons learned from global use. The framework is structured around three interconnected axes: health system challenges, digital health interventions and digital services and application types. It includes interventions for persons, health-care providers, health system managers and data services, alongside categories of digital applications and information systems. The classification is intended to support planning, implementation, investment analysis, research, interoperability considerations, policy development and the governance of digital health initiatives, thereby facilitating more consistent and effective use of digital technologies in health systems. ce3eed677ce1.doc: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
ce3eed677ce1.title: Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems
ce3eed677ce1.content: World Health Organization (2023). Digital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems. World Health Organization. TitleDigital adaptation kit for HIV: operational requirements for implementing WHO recommendations in digital systems AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2023-12-21 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240085138 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractThis second edition of the digital adaptation kit for HIV provides operational, software-neutral requirements to support the incorporation of WHO clinical, public health and data use recommendations into digital systems. Developed within the SMART Guidelines approach, it focuses on the content requirements for person-centred digital tracking and decision support systems used by health workers for HIV services in primary health care settings. The kit is intended to facilitate transparent, consistent and adaptable translation of narrative guidance into digital implementations while supporting interoperability and local customization. The publication organizes HIV-related requirements into eight components: health interventions and associated recommendations; generic personas; illustrative user scenarios; business processes and workflows; core data elements; decision support and scheduling logic; indicators and performance metrics; and high-level functional and non-functional requirements. It covers processes including HIV testing, pre-exposure prophylaxis, care and treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infant diagnosis, diagnostics, client follow-up, referral, and aggregate reporting and data use, with complementary operational resources provided in web annexes. TitleConsolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2026-7-22 Typebook PublisherWorld Health Organization ISBN9789240124233 (electronic version) Languageen AbstractHIV remains a major public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, despite the availability of effective treatment and prevention tools. Many evidence-based interventions are not implemented consistently or delivered in a timely manner, contributing to ongoing HIV transmission, advanced disease and preventable mortality. These consolidated WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations to strengthen HIV service delivery through people-centred, integrated and equitable approaches that improve access to care, continuity of treatment and accelerate progress towards ending AIDS as a public health threat. The publication consolidates all WHO recommendations on HIV service delivery issued between 2013 and 2025. It is intended to support the development of national and subnational policies, clinical guidelines and implementation guidance. It addresses key components of HIV service delivery, including linkage to care and antiretroviral therapy initiation, clinical follow-up and medication refills, adherence support and re-engagement in care, services for adolescents and young people, task sharing, decentralized service delivery, and integration with maternal and child health, tuberculosis, sexual and reproductive health, diabetes, hypertension and mental health services. Recommendations are classified as new, updated or revalidated according to WHO guideline development procedures. c29f83e22609.title: Understanding national health workforce accounts
c29f83e22609.content: World Health Organization (2017). Understanding national health workforce accounts. World Health Organization. TitleUnderstanding national health workforce accounts AuthorsWorld Health Organization Issued2017-12-31 Typereport PublisherWorld Health Organization Languageen AbstractUnderstanding National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) is an introductory guidance document developed by the World Health Organization to explain the purpose, policy relevance and structure of the National Health Workforce Accounts framework. The publication outlines how NHWA supports the standardization of health workforce information systems, improves the quality and comparability of data, and strengthens the evidence base for health workforce policy, planning and monitoring. Positioned within the context of universal health coverage, the Sustainable Development Goals, the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, and related international commitments, the document highlights the importance of reliable workforce information for addressing current and future health system challenges. The publication describes the benefits of NHWA at national, regional and global levels and presents key policy questions that can be informed through systematic workforce data collection and analysis. It introduces the health labour market framework used by NHWA, emphasizing workforce production, labour market flows, distribution, productivity and regulation. The document also summarizes the development process of the NHWA indicators and explains the modular structure of the framework, which comprises ten modules covering workforce stock, education, labour market dynamics, employment conditions, financing, governance, planning and information systems. Together, these elements provide a foundation for evidence-informed decision-making and strengthened health workforce monitoring.
